title: Completing forms and CVs
subtitle: fill in a form, date of birth, work experience
summary: Understand the formal language of official forms and name the sections of a CV.

lesson.heading: Types of form
rows: when you enter your name on an official list, e.g. at a school or college
when you apply to do a course of study
when you enter for an exam
for people from some countries when they enter the UK
when you officially ask to enter or leave a country

lesson.heading: The language of forms
lesson.text: When you **fill in** a form (= complete it), you meet formal expressions. In speech we say the same thing much more simply.

examples.text: **date of birth** = When were you born?
**place of birth** = Where were you born?
**country of origin** = Where do you come from?
**marital status** = Are you single or married?

lesson.heading: More form language
lesson.note: Your **signature** is the special way you have of writing your own name.

lesson.heading: What goes in a CV
lesson.text: If you apply for a job you send a letter and a **CV** (curriculum vitae; *resume* in American English). It gives your **personal details** - your name, address and email address.

examples.text: **personal details**: Leona Phillips, 18 Mansion Road, Beckington BE2 3RJ
**qualifications**: BA Honours degree in Media Studies
**work experience**: Trainee at Northern Radio Station, Jan-June 2007

lesson.heading: Interests, skills, aims and references
lesson.text: Your **interests** are what you enjoy doing. Your **skills** are abilities you have learned and practised. Your **career aims** are what you want to do in your future working life. A **reference** is a letter from someone who knows you, saying if you are suitable for the job.

examples.text: **interests**: I direct plays for a theatre group and help with a children's charity.
**skills**: the ability to speak a foreign language; computer skills; a driving licence.
**career aims**: I would like to become a radio producer.
**references**: a letter from Mr J. Tobin BA, MA (university tutor).

lesson.note: If you apply to university, they **require** a **personal statement** explaining why you want to go there and follow that course.

lesson.heading: Tips for writing a CV
lesson.text: A **tip** is a useful piece of advice. Keep your CV short, clear and correct. Say only what is **relevant** - connected to and useful for this particular job.

examples.text: A CV should be no longer than two pages; a personal statement no more than 45 lines.
**Type** your CV; handwriting is not suitable.
Keep it simple. Don't make it **complicated**.
If you will be working **on your own**, don't say you are good at working in a **team**.
examples.note: on your own = without others; a team = a group of people

lesson.text: You fill in (or complete) a form, and you sign it at the bottom. Both verbs are needed: an unsigned form is usually sent back.

exercises.prompt: You are just arriving in Britain from a country outside the European Union. What do you complete?
exercises.explanation: A landing card is for people entering the UK from some countries.

exercises.prompt: You are applying to do an English course at a school in Britain. What do you complete?
exercises.explanation: A registration or enrolment form puts your name on the list for a course.

exercises.prompt: You are going to do a Cambridge exam. What do you complete?
exercises.explanation: You enter for an exam with an entry form.

exercises.prompt: You want to travel to the United States this summer. What do you complete?
exercises.explanation: A visa application form is an official request to enter a country.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a CV with the right information.

pairs.right: BA Honours degree in Media Studies
Trainee at Northern Radio Station, Jan-June 2007
I would like to become a radio producer.
a letter from Mr J. Tobin, university tutor

exercises.prompt: Say it informally: 'What's your date of birth?' -> 'When ___?'
exercises.explanation: Date of birth = When were you born?

exercises.prompt: Say it informally: 'What's your country of origin?' -> 'Where do you ___?'
exercises.explanation: Country of origin = Where do you come from?

exercises.prompt: Say it informally: 'What's your marital status?' -> 'Are you ___?'
exercises.explanation: Marital status asks whether you are single or married.

exercises.prompt: Replace the words: 'Do I have to complete this form?' -> 'Do I have to ___ this form?'
exercises.explanation: Fill in a form = complete it.

exercises.prompt: Replace the words: 'Monica gave me a useful piece of advice.' -> 'Monica gave me a ___.'
exercises.explanation: A tip is a useful piece of advice.

exercises.prompt: Replace the words: 'I shall be alone most of the time.' -> 'I shall be ___ most of the time.'
Replace the words: 'I'm good at working as part of a group of people.' -> 'I'm good at working in a ___.'
exercises.explanation: A team is a group of people working together.

exercises.prompt: Is this good advice for a CV, or bad advice?

items.text: For an admin job, say you have computer skills.
Put a driving licence under skills.
One or two mistakes are fine.
Three pages is a good length.

exercises.statement: You can put 'travelling abroad' under career aims on your CV.
exercises.explanation: Travelling abroad is an interest, not a career aim. Career aims say what you want to do in your working life.
